marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q037.takeaway: The premotor cortex prepares posture and proximal muscles for a planned movement.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q037.displayText: The premotor cortex helps set posture at the start of a planned action and prepares the body for movement, especially through proximal limb muscles. It lies anterior to the precentral gyrus, receives parietal sensory input, and projects to primary motor cortex, brainstem reticular formation, and spinal cord. Its mirror neurons can respond during action observation as well as action performance.

rationales.b: Primary motor cortex executes commands and controls movement; the preparatory postural setting is attributed to premotor cortex.
rationales.c: ‘Frontal’ is too broad; the source identifies premotor cortex specifically.
rationales.d: Supplementary motor area helps organize internally generated movement sequences, whereas the described postural preparation and proximal-muscle orientation are premotor functions.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q038.takeaway: Spinal mass reflex produces strong flexor, not extensor, spasm.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q038.displayText: The vignette is a spinal mass reflex triggered by visceral distension after a high cord lesion. A large portion of skeletal muscle enters strong flexor spasm, while colon and bladder may evacuate, systolic pressure can exceed 200 mm Hg, and widespread sweating can occur. The false option substitutes extensor for flexor spasm.

rationales.a: Marked hypertension, sometimes with systolic pressure above 200 mm Hg, is among the source-listed mass-reflex effects.
rationales.c: Profuse sweating over large body areas is a recognized effect listed for spinal mass reflex.
rationales.d: The source states the colon and bladder are likely to evacuate during this widespread spinal discharge.
